children: Anil Rego, Founder and Fund Manager at Right Horizons, believes India’s growth remains structurally resilient, although consistently maintaining the current 7.5-8 percent quarterly growth rate may become challenging if oil prices remain elevated.

“Our base case would be some moderation rather than a significant growth slowdown. The domestic investment and consumption cycle remains sufficiently strong to absorb a reasonable amount of external volatility,” he said in an interview with Moneycontrol.
At this stage, he believes 12-15 percent earnings growth for FY27 remains achievable, although the composition of that growth will matter considerably.

Anil Rego continues to see an earnings recovery developing across financials, autos, industrials, capital goods and selected consumer businesses. “That is consistent with our view that the market is transitioning from a valuation-led phase towards an earnings-led phase,” he said.
Do you believe rising interest rates and risk-free yields are creating a challenging environment for equities?

Rising risk-free yields are clearly raising the hurdle rate for equities, particularly for businesses where valuations are dependent on earnings far into the future. US Treasury yields recently moved close to the 5 percent mark amid renewed inflation concerns, higher oil prices and expectations of tighter monetary policy. In such an environment, investors naturally demand a higher earnings yield from equities, which can constrain valuation multiples.

However, we would differentiate between valuation pressure and an earnings problem. In India, a significant part of the valuation adjustment has already happened. MSCI India has declined over 5 percent in 2026, even as MSCI Asia and Emerging Markets gained 22 percent and 23 percent, respectively. Consequently, India's relative valuation premium has compressed materially.

More importantly, earnings are beginning to improve. Nifty 50 profits grew 18 percent YoY in Q1FY27, the strongest growth in 10 quarters. Therefore, while higher yields can limit broad-based multiple expansion, companies capable of delivering superior earnings growth can still generate returns. We believe this increasingly becomes a stock-picker's market rather than a liquidity-driven market.
In addition, will this have a major impact on the real estate sector?

Rising interest rates can create near-term pressure on real estate by increasing home-loan EMIs and weakening affordability, particularly when property prices have already risen significantly. This makes the mid-income segment more sensitive than premium housing.

However, we do not expect a major structural impact at this stage, as underlying demand remains resilient—housing sales by value grew 11 percent YoY in H1CY26, while unsold inventory remains comfortable at around 20 months. The bigger risk is the combination of higher borrowing costs and elevated ticket sizes. Developers that maintain affordability and have strong balance sheets should therefore be relatively better positioned.
Do you rule out the possibility of a US-Iran deal even before the US midterm elections?

We would not rule out the possibility of a US-Iran deal before the US midterm elections. There are economic and political incentives for both sides to avoid a prolonged confrontation, particularly given the implications for crude oil prices, inflation and global growth. For the US, some de-escalation could help contain energy prices and inflationary pressures ahead of the elections, while Iran could benefit from sanctions relief and improved economic conditions.

However, geopolitical negotiations remain highly unpredictable, and significant differences between the two sides persist. Markets will probably respond positively even to de-escalation rather than waiting for a formal agreement, because the immediate transmission mechanism is crude oil. Brent is currently around $95 per barrel, and any credible reduction in the risk to Hormuz supply could remove a meaningful geopolitical premium from oil.
Do you think the economic growth seen in recent quarters will be sustainable going forward, considering the ongoing tensions in West Asia and elevated oil prices?
We believe India's growth remains structurally resilient, although maintaining the current 7.5-8 percent quarterly growth rate consistently may become challenging if oil stays elevated.

India's GDP grew 7.8 percent YoY in Q1FY27, comfortably ahead of the RBI's 7 percent estimate and the market expectation of around 7.1 percent. What is encouraging is the composition of this growth. Private investment increased nearly 12 percent, consumption grew 7.1 percent, manufacturing expanded 9.2 percent, and financial services grew more than 12 percent.

We are also beginning to see the growth engine broaden beyond government capex. Gross fixed capital formation increased to 34.3 percent of GDP from 31.4 percent a year ago, while private-sector investment is gaining momentum.

The principal near-term vulnerability remains crude. India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude requirements, which means sustained oil prices around $95-100 can transmit through the current account, inflation, currency and eventually corporate margins.

Hence, our base case would be some moderation rather than a significant growth slowdown. The domestic investment and consumption cycle remains sufficiently strong to absorb a reasonable amount of external volatility.
Despite these headwinds, do you still expect 12-15 percent Nifty earnings growth in the current fiscal year?

At this stage, we believe 12-15 percent earnings growth for FY27 remains achievable, although the composition of that growth will matter considerably. Q1 has provided a strong starting point. Nifty 50 PAT grew 18 percent YoY, versus expectations of roughly 10 percent, marking the strongest growth in 10 quarters. Nineteen sectors exceeded estimates and the upgrade-to-downgrade ratio improved to around 1.5x.

Importantly, earnings revisions are also beginning to stabilise. We therefore continue to see an earnings recovery developing across financials, autos, industrials, capital goods and selected consumer businesses. That is consistent with our view that the market is transitioning from a valuation-led phase towards an earnings-led phase.

The biggest risk to the 12-15 percent assumption would be oil remaining close to or above $100 for an extended period. That would put greater pressure on margins in energy-intensive sectors, consumer businesses, aviation and other crude-linked industries.
Has the HDFC Bank stock already priced in all the recent negatives?

Our view remains that a significant part of the recent negatives is already reflected in HDFC Bank’s stock price, given the sharp correction and valuation de-rating. The stock is now valued at around 1.3–1.4x FY28/Sept-28E adjusted book value, which appears more reasonable for a strong underlying franchise.

However, a meaningful re-rating would require improvement in operating performance and greater clarity on leadership. Deposit mobilisation remains critical for supporting loan growth and margin recovery, while governance and succession remain key monitorables.
Do you expect significant investments across the energy and AI ecosystems going forward?

We believe AI and energy will increasingly become interconnected capex themes rather than independent investment cycles. AI infrastructure requires enormous computing capacity, but equally importantly it requires reliable electricity, transmission, cooling and storage infrastructure. India is increasingly participating in this build-out. Private investment data already point towards significant capex in AI, semiconductors, manufacturing and data centres, with Google and Amazon together having committed more than $40 billion towards Indian data-centre infrastructure.

The second-order opportunity is power. Data centres, manufacturing, EVs and electrification will require considerable investments across generation, transmission, storage and grid infrastructure. India is simultaneously targeting 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and exploring a very substantial expansion of nuclear power to 100 GW by 2047, which is estimated to require around $210 billion of investment.
Transmission is particularly important. Recent projects are already being designed specifically to move several gigawatts of renewable and storage capacity into major consumption centres.

Hence, we see this as a multi-year ecosystem opportunity encompassing power generation, renewables, transmission equipment, transformers, cables, storage, cooling systems, data centres, cloud infrastructure and semiconductor-related manufacturing. The opportunity is likely to be substantial, although stock selection remains critical because valuations in some of these segments already discount a meaningful part of the long-term growth opportunity.
